title: Vitamins in Human Body
summary: Essential micronutrients required for growth, development, and overall health. Vitamins cannot be synthesized by the body in sufficient amounts and must be obtained through diet.

children.title: Vitamin Classification
children.summary: Vitamins are classified into two major categories based on their solubility properties: fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins. This classification affects how they are absorbed, transported, stored, and excreted in the body.

children.title: Fat-Soluble Vitamins
children.summary: Absorbed along with fats in the diet and stored in the body's fatty tissue and liver. Include vitamins A, D, E, and K. Can accumulate in the body and don't need to be consumed daily.

children.title: Vitamin A (Retinol)
children.summary: Critical for vision, immune function, skin health, and cellular communication. Deficiency can cause night blindness.

children.title: Vitamin D (Calciferol)
children.summary: Essential for calcium absorption, bone health, immune function, and mood regulation. Can be synthesized by skin when exposed to sunlight.

children.title: Vitamin E (Tocopherol)
children.summary: Powerful antioxidant that protects cells from damage, supports immune function, and promotes skin health.

children.title: Vitamin K (Phylloquinone)
children.summary: Essential for blood clotting and bone metabolism. Helps wounds heal properly.

children.title: Water-Soluble Vitamins
children.summary: Dissolve in water and are not stored in the body. Excess amounts are excreted in urine, so they need to be consumed regularly. Include vitamin C and the B-complex vitamins.

children.title: Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid)
children.summary: Powerful antioxidant essential for immune function, collagen synthesis, wound healing, and iron absorption. Humans cannot produce it naturally.

children.title: B-Complex Vitamins
children.summary: Group of 8 vitamins that play vital roles in energy production, brain function, and cell metabolism. Work together to convert food into energy.

children.title: B1 (Thiamine)
children.summary: Essential for glucose metabolism and nerve, muscle, and heart function.

children.title: B12 (Cobalamin)
children.summary: Critical for red blood cell formation, neurological function, and DNA synthesis. Found primarily in animal products.

children.title: Dietary Sources
children.summary: Vitamins are obtained through a balanced diet including fruits, vegetables, whole grains, dairy products, and proteins. Some vitamins can be synthesized (like Vitamin D from sunlight) or produced by gut bacteria (like Vitamin K).

children.title: Plant-Based Sources
children.summary: Fruits, vegetables, legumes, nuts, seeds, and whole grains provide most water-soluble vitamins and some fat-soluble ones (like Vitamin E and K).

children.title: Animal-Based Sources
children.summary: Meat, fish, eggs, and dairy products are excellent sources of Vitamin B12, D, A, and some B vitamins.

children.title: Deficiency Disorders
children.summary: Insufficient vitamin intake can lead to various health conditions. Common deficiencies include Vitamin D (bone problems), B12 (anemia), and C (scurvy).
